text: Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Lauren Chernoff, and I am calling this June 3rd, 2026, Specialized Programs and Centers Committee meeting to order. I am joined by my colleague, Mr. Pepper, and Ms. Donahue will be absent for today's meeting. We are going to start. We have a very full house today. Welcome to all our guests. We're so happy to see you. We have some students here as well. So we're going to begin with item 2.01, which is procedures for

public comment. So we value the public comment process, and we are so glad that you are here today. We have three speakers, and we're going to give you each two minutes. So I will call you, and you can come up and just make sure that you turn on your microphone so that we have you on the record, okay? The first speaker is Sana Saeed.

Good evening, board members. My name is Sana, and I'm a student in the biomedical technology pathway at MATA, the Monroe Advanced Technical Academy. Before we share our experiences tonight, I want to take a moment to make sure everyone has a clear picture of what MATA actually is, because I think context is essential to everything that follows. MATA is a specialized career and technical education program within the Academies of Loudoun. MATA offers programs like biomedical technology, auto collision, and cosmetology, each designed to give students

professional-level training in a specific field. These pathways are either one year or two years in length. Students spend six hours every other day inside a single specialized program. Let me put that in perspective. In a course in one's home school, a student accumulates roughly 128 hours of instruction over the course of a single academic year. On the other hand, one year in a MATA pathway totals approximately 540 hours. A two-year pathway,

like biomedical technology, totals to around 1,080 hours, nearly nine times the instructional time of a course taken at home schools. This time commitment exists for a reason. All MATA pathways send their students off with collegiate-level skills, with some even having end-of-course certifications, which include CNA or an HVAC certification. These skill sets allow students to directly carry their qualifications in the workforce the moment they graduate high school.

Opportunities like that don't exist in most of the county. So when we talk about MATA, we're talking about half of a student's high school career dedicated to a single professional pathway. Now, I want to be transparent with the board about something, because I think it matters to the credibility of everything I've just said. I entered the biomedical technology pathway through the lottery system. I did not go through the original process of submitting an essay or my academic scores. My number was drawn, and I was given a seat.

I am genuinely grateful for that opportunity. Being in this program has confirmed for me that biomedical science is exactly where I want to be, and I do not take lightly the fact that I get to be here. I don't think that the system any of us ultimately wants for something- Thank you. Your time is up. But you can email us the rest of your comments. Okay. We would love to hear the rest of them. Thank you. Thank you for being here. All right. Our next speaker is Sahil Sambagi.

Good evening, board members. My name is Sahil, and I'm a current student in the biomedical technology pathway at MATA. My path began here in sophomore year when I applied for the Intro to Health and Medical Sciences program under the previous non-lottery-based admissions system. That process asked me to demonstrate my interest and articulate clearly why I wanted to pursue this field. It asked me before I ever set foot in the program to decide whether this was truly where I wanted to go.

I went through this process, displayed my passion, and spent a year in IHMS building that foundation. When I later applied to continue in biomedical technology, the system changed to a lottery. I want to be clear, I got in, and I was fortunate to do so. But I want to spend my time tonight talking about not my own admission, but what I observed in the classroom during my time in IHMS, because I think it speaks to something important.

What the non-lottery process created was a room full of students who had already made a decision. Everyone around me had been asked the hard question before they arrived. "Is this the field you want to dedicate yourself to?" And they'd answer it with intention. That shared sense of purpose shaped everything. It shaped how students engaged with the material. It shaped how we supported each other. It shaped the energy of the classroom where everyone had chosen to be there. I want to be careful here, because I can only speak to what I personally witnessed.

But what I observed in that environment was students who were not only present, they were invested. They asked questions beyond the curriculum. They talked about where this pathway was going to take them. The program brought out a level of dedication that I genuinely believe was connected to the fact that everyone in that room was devoted to their spot. This is why demonstrated interest was required. Not exclusivity, not hierarchy. A room full of students who knew why they were there and who pushed each other

because of it. When I applied to biomedical technology and the system had already changed, I entered a program that still had the foundation because many of my classmates were from that IHMS program. But what I noticed was that some of my new classmates seemed to be encountering the reality that this commitment for the first time, not because they lacked ability, but because they had not had the opportunity to decide whether this was truly for them. I'll let my colleague speak more on that. Thank you. Appreciate you.
All right. We have one last speaker, and it is Anish Ramasami.

Good evening, board members. My name is Anish, and I'm a student in the biomedical technology pathway at MATA. Like Sahil, I entered Intro to Health and Medical Sciences my sophomore year through the non-lottery admission system. I made the case for why this was the field I wanted to pursue, and I meant every word of it because I had genuinely asked myself the question before I put pen to paper.When I applied to continue in the biomedical technology pathway, the system had changed. I entered through the lottery, and I want to be honest with the board. I am grateful that my number came up.

I am grateful every single day that I get to be in this program. But there is something that gratitude can never be able to quiet, and that is the reason I'm standing here tonight. I watch classmates from my intro to health and medical sciences pathway, people I'd spent a year learning alongside, people who had done the exact same process that I had gone through, not get into biomedical technology. Not because their passion had changed, not because their work had slipped, not because anything about their commitment to this field wavered. Because their number wasn't drawn.

I sat with that, and I still sit with it, because I know what those students put in. I was there when they put it in. I saw how much this pathway meant to them, and I know that this skill set, and I know that they know that there was a skill set waiting at the end of it, the kind that doesn't exist anywhere else in this county, was something they wanted just as badly as I did. And I am in this classroom, and they are not. Not because I wanted it more, but because I was lucky. I want to be very clear about what I'm saying. I'm not saying that access doesn't matter. I'm not saying that this program should only belong to certain students.

I believe with my whole heart that every student who has a genuine interest in these fields deserves a path towards them. That's not what brought us here tonight. What brought us here is something quieter and harder to name. It is the feeling of sitting in a classroom knowing that the person next to you is not truly immersed in the program, and knowing that somewhere outside of this building, there is someone who has demonstrated passion and commitment to this program and was never given the chance to attend. It is the question of whether luck, pure arbitrary luck, is the right mechanism for allocating an opportunity this rare and this significant.

We trust the board with that question. We are not here to tell you what the answer will look like. We are here because we lived it, and because we believe you deserve to hear it from the students who did. Thank you. Thank you. You made it under the wire. I want to thank you so much for being here. I think it takes a lot of courage and bravery to come and speak at a school board meeting, and we really value your perspective. You're in the trenches. You're living it every day, and so I'm very, very grateful for your presence here today. And to the educators that encouraged you and brought you, thank you so much. This matters. So thank you.

All righty. With that, we will move on to item 3.01, the approval of the draft minutes from our May 6th meeting. Do I have any changes or a motion? Madam Chair, I move to approve the draft minutes from the May 6th, 2026, meeting of the Specialized Programs and Centers Committee. And I will second that. All those in favor? Aye. Aye. It passes unanimously. And now we will move on to item four, which is our only action item of the night, 4.01, Charter

School Annual Technology Services and Support Services Contracts. And we have staff here to speak to that if you have anything to add. But if not, I'm actually going to just go ahead and make a motion to move the Charter School Annual Technology Services and Support Services Contracts to the full board. Do I have a second? Second. Excellent. Is there any discussion? I will just make some brief comments.

I have been in communication with our charter schools, and I think we are all in agreement that the timeline of this is what is key and needs to move forward. And I appreciate all of staff really illuminating that context and that the changes really are minimal. I think where the growing pains literal that we're feeling is that as systems come closer to failure, the worry that this contract could become unsustainable is what most of the charter schools

are worried about. And I think that that is a conversation that we can continue to have while we still move this forward. And so I will be supporting moving it forward, and I believe we have their support behind us at this time, and I look forward to level setting, as we mentioned last time, on just contracts in general and getting everybody on the same page so that we can work towards a more efficient and realistic expectation in terms of those things. So it has been properly moved and seconded.

All those in favor of passing this to the full board, say aye. Aye. Aye. That passes two to zero, with Ms. Donahue absent from the vote, which I did not say for the minutes, but it's the same thing. Ms. Sandra, you got that? Okay. All right. So that will move forward. And then tonight, we just have one information item. It is jam-packed, I believe. So we will have our guests and speakers move to the microphones, and it is a special programs
yearly update. This is part two, and I'm going to pass it off to Ms. Kathryn Clark, Director of Academic Programs, and she will introduce our guests.

Good evening. As everyone gets settled, I'll kick us off. Thank you for having us back. This is part two of our special programs yearly overview. This evening, we have all three of our ACL programs. We have our Academy of Engineering and Technology. We have Academy of Science, our MATA program, along with our NJROTC that we weren't able to get to last time, and ACCESS Academy. So as we move through the presentation, I'll have each

individual introduce themselves, and we are going to kick off with Dr. Grazida with NJROTC. Thank you, Ms. Clark. Good evening. Oh. Surprised? I was like, "What?" I didn't see you come in. That was great. That was awesome.

Well, good evening, everyone. I'd like to give a few updates for our NJROTC program. Next slide. Of course, we have NJROTC at one of our high schools, Loudoun County High School. Rising ninth-grade students, public, private, and homeschool can show interest in this programOut-of-zone students are selected through the special programs lottery process. Starting the '26-'27 school year, there are 25 seats

for the incoming freshman class available to zone Loudoun County High School students to have access to this program. Those are our students that come from J. Lupton Simpson Middle School. And this is a four-year commitment, and students who are from out of zone become full-time students at Loudoun County High School. Next slide. So what we're looking at here is

entered in ninth-grade students going from Naval Science 1 to Naval Science 2. The data is approximately September 30th, 2024 to September 30th, 2025. So that's why we have just a single year. You can see that we have a 75% retention rate for those students for that one year that we've captured this data. Next slide, please. So this year was an eventful year. We had the annual

NJROTC military inspection, was actually canceled because of a snow day. And so what we had to do was tell the admiral that we will submit the inspection via video. And so we had a plethora of students and staff from the CTA division develop that video, and the inspection was really well-received by the admiral. They were thoroughly impressed by that video. So we're happy to share that with you all later on if you're interested.

We're looking at getting some snippets later on for recruiting material. It was quite impressive. We had four NJROTC SeaPerch teams competing at the national level this past weekend. Three teams actually participated at the University of Maryland this past weekend. And I want to report that the Sea Turtles, one of our teams, earned third place in the High School Mission Course competition and fifth place in the Technical Design Report category. So very

cool stuff with our SeaPerch. If you haven't seen it, it's underwater robotics. The team did have a chance to practice here locally in Leesburg at the SwimKids school. It's quite impressive, so I invite you all to come out and check it out. We had multiple district ceremonial events supported, one school board presentation by the Color Guard, as you all saw. They also supported the school business partnership breakfast, which was

fantastic. And then we had 100% program compliance with uniforms, curriculum credit, and certified instructor staffing. Next slide, please. So just a high-level snapshot of achievements, highlights, and opportunities. We had two cadets earn service academy appointments so far. Captain Schoen is expecting more, but as of right now, we have two to report. The cadet leadership team has been selected for the '26-'27 school year.

We're very excited with that leadership team. As you all know, this is student-led. They lead all nine of our teams in the morning, and they have opportunities to lead during class time. Family engagement, families participated in structured intake meetings, ongoing outreach supported informed enrollment choices. Mr. Schaefer led several meetings at Loudoun County High School, in the cafeteria and the auditorium, and they were really well-received by the public. It was really great.

Our inspection was successfully completed, as I just relayed. Program operations sustained despite restrictions. You all might have been aware that uniforms were restricted earlier this year. That ban has been lifted, and our students are in full uniform again. We did get a distinguished unit status, expanded through academy access, as I said. Cadets competed in the NJROTC competitions, as I said.

And this past Sunday, our Color Guard was represented at the Nationals game. So we have had some really great opportunities to show off our NJROTC program. That's all that I have to present for you all tonight. I'm happy to answer any questions that you have. Thank you so much. Mr. Pepper. So let me begin with thank you for the presentation. Sure. It's always good to see that our NJROTC program is doing well, because

from what I see, it looks like it's doing really well. You had mentioned there are 25 zone slots. So those are students that are directly going from Simpson up to Loudoun County High School. Yes. How many total slots are in the program? Fifty per year. So we can have 25 from out of- That is correct ... out of zone. Okay. Just want to make sure that I- Yes sir ... had those numbers right. And then that one slide, even though it's the one-year cohort, that's just one year of the cohort? Yes, sir.

So I'm assuming that we could track that data over multiple years as it kind of builds out. Yes. Okay. And then I do want to know about these uniforms. Why could they not wear the uniforms? There was an edict sent out by Navy command, due to issues abroad- Okay ... that students in NJROTC or JROTC programs not wear their uniforms. And that ban was lifted at the end of April. Okay. Thank you. You're welcome.

It's nothing we did. Yes. Okay. No, not at all. All right. I have a few questions. This program happens to sit in Leesburg, so I had a chance to follow up with Dr. Luttrell and Captain Schoen. Is that how you say it? Yes. Is that right? Okay. Just to sort of get a pulse on where things are at. Again, I haven't really had a deep dive on these things. I

think you're going to sense a theme tonight from me, and the theme is to lottery or not to lottery. And maybe it's in the middle. I don't know. But-I think that there has been a little bit of a struggle with the transition to the lottery, and I don't think that's a secret to the team, because it sounds like you guys have been really engaged with them, and they've been very appreciative. But I do wonder how we can reflect on that and think about that going forward in

terms of... And our MATIS students also spoke to this tonight, and I sort of thought I've heard this, this week before, but it was about JROTC, is the level of commitment, the desire to be involved in something that is military-driven, the hours that it requires, the discipline, and the structure. I agree with the students. I think you said it so delicately that it's not about we don't want kids to have access. We want kids to have access, but we also want to

maximize the integrity of the program. And something that has struck me over the last few months being on this committee is just how precious it is to have a true JROTC program here in Loudoun County. Mm. Just the difficulties that we have faced in trying to get a program outside of that. So I guess I want us to think about, and maybe you can shed a little bit of light about what some of that tension has been in terms of making that transition.

But how can we keep the integrity and authenticity of the program while still informing people that are applying to the lottery about what the commitment really is? And I know we do information nights, and I know we do things like that, but through the selection process before, it's my understanding that the family sat down, they had a full conversation about the requirements. Is that something that we still do, that we can still do to make sure that we are

keeping kids in the program? Because I know that also is impacting staffing which is another thing that has come up. So just kind of in general, if you could speak to sort of what that journey has been like as we have transitioned to the lottery. Absolutely. It's a great question. And, yes, there has been a lot of conversation about the lottery and how that has impacted student interest, student enrollment. The meetings that Mr. Schaefer set up for the families who

were accepted into the program for the '26, '27 year, those were mandatory meetings, so all the families did have to attend. We did have near perfect attendance. There was one family who was not able to attend, and they decided to decline acceptance into the program. So in essence, we do have 100% participation in the mandatory meetings. The program overview was given by Captain Shone, Gunny, Chief Martinez.

The student leaders, the cadet leaders for '26, '27, also participated in answering questions and guiding families through the actual program. So they were there to answer all questions. They stayed there extensively. Dr. Luttrell was at both meetings. So I feel like we've given all the information and answered all the questions that the families have had. Mr. Schaefer and I continue to be on correspondence with families, with Captain Shone about uniform pickup, about what summer

PT is going to look like. So, we're still engaging in those conversations, and I feel like our communication has been on target. I appreciate that. And I do think that as we continue down this path, I think we have to continue to be reflective about where these different structures fit. And I'm not sure I'm totally sold that a lottery system for JROTC is the right approach, but I also see the benefits

of casting a wider net, if you will, and to offer selection to students that may not even-- I think there's a lot of kids that could benefit from a very disciplined approach that they might not realize that otherwise. I'm also hearing from my community that there are some kids that did get left behind, and they really had always thought that this was going to be their path. Sure. And Mr. Slevin and I were speaking earlier, maybe that includes some

conversations about how we look at kids at the base school and what percentage of the slots they get if we were to change that. So I'm open to the dialogue. I think the process right now is the process, obviously. But I think over the next year, I would like to learn more and understand a little bit better where some of those needs might arise and how we could evaluate that. And I would also be interested in the data year over year just to

see that transition of are we holding on to kids. I think 75% is decent, but I'd like to see that be a little bit higher. Mm-hmm. So, is there any other...? Yes, Ms. Clark. I just want to add to that 75%. There wasn't a process prior to this year for zoned students to apply. So that was part of what we initiated, is all students had to put in to apply.

Before they were just scheduling Loudoun County students into Naval 1. So we worked diligently, special programs and Dr. Grubbs, to make sure we had a clean process. So that 75% might've been kids who were Loudoun County High School students who only took one year of that course and did not go through the formal process. So, again, we also were not using our system where we now have student

needs for all students in all programs. So we've kind of come a long way, so we will have that data to show who's been in the program over time for all programs. I appreciate that clarification, and I think that's the kind of data that will really help guide us in the future about these processes and seeing where we are. And just to put it on the record, I know that of course, they always want more instructors, and I think part of that retention rate would help

lead to the numbers that they would need to have more instructors. So retention is also important to staffing. Correct?Is that a fair statement? Yes. Okay. For every 50 students we have in the program, we get an instructor. Okay. So right now, we have three instructors. We have over 150 students in the program. So right now we're meeting all the needs of the students. Okay, great. Mm-hmm. I appreciate you all so much. I look forward to learning more, and thank you for being here. Thank you.

All right, Ms. Clark, I'll let you pass it over to the Academies group. All right. Awesome. Yes, we're going to pass it right on to Academy of Engineering and Technology, and Mr. Markley. Good evening, Ms. Chernoff and Mr. Pepper. It is a joy to be here and kick off the academy's presentation. Not to steal Ms. Chang's thunder, because our two programs are very similar, but the Academy of Engineering Technology also culminates in student research. And so AET, as we affectionately call it, has three

different pathways: information technology, also AKA computer science, engineering, and entrepreneurship. Those are four-year pathways where students can enter as ninth graders. AET is unique from MATA and AOS in that there's two different entry points. Ninth graders can come for the four-year pathway. We also have advanced AET in IT and engineering fields for rising juniors. They are research-focused programs. They culminate in students conducting independent research, although it looks different than bench science.

There's technical research and also students in entrepreneurial pathway pitch projects, and so it is a great program, and it's great to see where our students can really explore and live up to that motto that we have, our mission of making meaningful contributions in the fields of STEM: science, technology, engineering, and math. On the next slide, we have some data, retention data. I'll try to give this a little context. What you're looking at for each year is the year that cohort entered

as freshmen. So when we see the 2022 year, these are our current seniors. So we had 100% retention as of September 30th of that year for all the freshmen in that class were still there. Over the course of their four years, you see that the size of that cohort has decreased. And so I'm going to talk a little bit more about that when we discuss entrepreneurship on the next slide of opportunities for AET. But for example, of the 30 students who have not stayed all the

way through their senior year, 19 of them are from the one specific pathway, and so I want to talk a little bit more about that. When you look at the class who will be seniors this coming year, you see that drop again from sophomore to junior year. Of that 11%, two-thirds of them are from a single pathway where we're seeing they're not continuing beyond their sophomore year. And so I want to speak to that. But overall retention is mostly positive. When we go in the school year, AET has always had excellent retention. We shared that data

last year at this meeting, and so overall very positive, but there's one specific use case I think that's worth exploring as a possible opportunity for AET. And so of course, 2024, 2025, those are our current sophomores and freshmen. We still have high retention with historically similar data. So there's a lot of text on this slide, and so I'm going to try to speak to it casually without reading from it. There are amazing accomplishments that can be shared, of course.

Explore, research, collaborate, and innovate. Those are the four pillars on which our mission is built around. Students do incredible research. We recently had our ACL Research Symposium at the end of May. It is breathtaking to see the research that students are doing across all three of the academy's curricular programs. Our students have experienced success at the Regional Science and Engineering Fair. And we had, for the first time, this is very exciting, one of our advanced AET student pairs conducted a research project and were ultimately named ISEF

finalists and then placed at ISEF. And so it's really cool to see students in our two-year pathway independently taking on a research project, being mentored by our faculty, and experiencing high external validation for it. We, of course, don't believe that the external validation is the purpose of doing research. We really think it is about all the skills that our students gain throughout that process, but they are successful there. We have international collaborations and research partnerships.

This was an inaugural year for AET to have this curriculum-embedded research partnership. This is similar to what AOS has had for many years in Singapore that Ms. Chang will talk about, I am sure. And we had students that are juniors in the engineering and IT pathways collaborating with peers, and we're getting ready on June 16th to travel over to Austria to go present that year-long research and also have some cultural exchange activities. I also need to shout out our Computer Science Honor

Society, as well as our two faculty leads that lead that program, Ms. Erin Whisler and Ms. Toby Jalloh. This group of students, under their leadership, has led high-quality STEM experiences for nearly 1,000 students this year. Between the Hour of Code for the Propel and Level Up programs, as well as the academy's Hackathon, and recently, the academy's Informatics Tournament. In addition to that, students from those programs have also contributed to community outreach support in the Robotics Showcase and Amazon Girls in

STEM. So those are not our events. We don't own them, but those CSHS students, among other academy student volunteers, have been instrumental in making these opportunities for our community happen, and I just want to celebrate those accomplishments. Family engagement is always a thing. Whenever you interface with the entirety of Loudoun County Public Schools, we have quite a geographic spread in our building. And so each year before the school year starts, our ninth graders, our faculty goes out and visit their rising ninth graders for

advisory visits to answer any questions they might have. We might invite those students to come into the building. It might be home visits. It might be at a library, depending on what families choose to do. And it's a great way for us to start getting kids in the door, helping them feel seen. We had the inaugural AET Entrepreneurship Gala recently on May 18th. Previously, students in the entrepreneurship program, when they did their final pitch, it was a during the school day event. We do have our shark tank, our board of advisors that was there, but it wasn't open to families, it wasn't open to the community, and it was great to have the

support of Dr. SpenceDr. Ellis, Dr. Grubbs, and others who came out to support the Entrepreneurship Gala in a way to showcase the amazing work that our students are doing. Our project that was selected made the quarterfinals of the National Pitch Competition, so they were one of the top 25 projects in the nation in terms of their business pitch for their entitled business, Funk Off. It was a very catchy name. For the second year in a row, we've had an admitted student orientation

that is different in that both Ms. Chang and I have led special information sessions to launch that visit to the academies to really try to help provide some clarity of information to families and to students, answer some of the questions that we know are frequently asked, and then, of course, I already spoke about our research symposium. Some major highlights in AET this year and for the academies in general, ACL Raptor Time is a new structure that we have to support students.

Students sacrifice a lot to come to the academies in each of our three programs. They frequently give up a study hall. So what we've done is one A day and B day each week, students have the opportunity to go get specialized support in learning labs for science, math, or research teachers, or engineering or computer science. And then we also have places where students can take reassessments because not every student has access to transportation before or after school, and it's a dedicated time where they don't have to give up lunch to go get that support. It was highly successful, and I'm sure there's lots of conversations about how it

can continue to develop or expand. For AET looking to next school year, advanced AET, that two-year pathway, is moving to A day. This is a significant accomplishment because the juniors and seniors in that program have always attended on the same day, B day, as the freshmen and sophomores in the four-year program. That's contributed feeling like a little bit like of a side, like afterthought, and not being there with their peers. It also affects our home schools' planning because they have juniors and seniors

now that are attending the academies for at least AOS and ADT, or AT specifically, on different days. And so this is a big change. It opens up course flexibility for those students in those programs. We couldn't offer all the science electives to them, and so now that they are attending on the same day as their four-year counterparts, they'll be in some of the same classes together, and they have the full access to all the course offerings that we have as a program. So that's a big step in terms of access and opportunity next year. We have enhanced student choice and electives.

Previously all juniors in our program took AP Physics in the Academy of Engineering Technology. We've opened up now. Over 80% of our juniors are still going to take that course because they believe that fits their career path. But providing that flexibility helps because one of the secondary reasons why we're seeing so much attrition from sophomore to junior year was that forced move into AP Physics, where some students didn't feel like their math skills were ready. Because not only do they have to understand calculus, but they're now applying in that course, and so that extra year of growth gives them a chance

to, number one, choose the science course that they're most interested in and maybe have some mathematical maturation before they take that course. And then we also have a revised scheduling framework for AET specifically going into the next year to provide some common planning time. One of the mottos of the academies when the building was constructed was unintentional collisions. We now are trying to create some intentional collisions to support our teacher collaboration and ultimately be responsive to our students' needs.

And then looking at opportunities, so some programming considerations. AP Physics C, Electricity and Magnetism is not currently offered. We have submitted the request through the science office and teaching and learning, so that is being pushed out there as a possible additional course that students can take. It's another high-level course, but there is a lot of interest in that field specifically. Looking at entrepreneurship pathway evolution. So if we went back to that data, you see that drop between sophomore and junior

year. So again, 31 of our 50 entrepreneurship seniors this year still remain at the academies. Of those 19 who did not continue to their junior year, many of them said they wanted to continue with their business interests or things, or some of them were looking for courses that weren't available because of the day they were scheduled at academies. We have some thoughts about how inverting the pathway might help in terms of when they take their entrepreneurship coursework and when

they take their technical classes in retaining those students for all four years. And then also looking at the IT pathway evolution. Computer science has changed a lot in the last decade, and so as that field continues to evolve, our courses and how we integrate with computer science courses across the county and provide access to advanced computing opportunities, we are constantly evaluating and looking for refinements there. And then international research. We continue to seek those opportunities or evaluate the ones that we currently have
